extracted.intended_audience: mathematics teachers and educators (school and university), curriculum designers, professors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for how to teach mathematics effectively, emphasizing concrete examples, connections to physics and modeling, avoidance of sterile axiomatization, and cultivation of geometric and problem-solving intuition across school and university levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as part of physics / connect to reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics is a part of physics; it should be taught as the sector of physics where experiments are cheap, keeping close contact with physical reality and examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples like the Jacobi identity, paraboloids, parametric curves, Riemann surfaces and elliptic integrals to show how mathematical facts are experimental-like discoveries and connected to the real world. Avoid cutting mathematics off from physics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the experimental/empirical cycle (observation–model–test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer the scientific scheme observation → model → investigation of the model → conclusions → testing by observations rather than substituting it with definition → theorem → proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach modelling and the necessity of subsequent control of deductions by experiment; show limits of models and stress that axioms are idealisations with relative validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-axiomatization and scholastic abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present mathematics as sterile axiomatic systems detached from intuition and applications; avoid 'ugly scholastic pseudo-mathematics' that isolates students from reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: giving unmotivated definitions, proving trivialities purely for raising formality, or emphasising abstract generalisations (Hodge structures, Jacobi varieties) at the cost of basic geometric intuition. Illustrative failure: pupils answering '3+2' to 'what is 2+3?'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivate definitions with examples and historical/contextual development
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce definitions via the historical or concrete concepts from which they arose so they are understandable and meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: define a group historically as a collection of transformations/one-to-one mappings closed under composition and inversion rather than as a dry set with axioms. Use the historical route to give motivation and intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach through concrete geometric/visual intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Use geometry and visual models (e.g., determinants as oriented volumes, manifolds as graphs) to make abstract notions clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show determinant as the (oriented) volume of a parallelepiped; define smooth manifolds as k-dimensional submanifolds of Euclidean space locally graphs of smooth maps; encourage drawing of curves and surfaces (hypocycloids, paraboloids, parametric curves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stress modeling limitations and sensitivity to assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize that mathematical models idealise reality and that small parameter/axiom changes or long deduction chains may drastically change conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples such as the Malthus equation and uniqueness theorems to show where model conclusions exceed practical accuracy; explain why long fancy deduction chains are less reliable for real-world application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experiments, numerical checks and examples to control errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Combat accumulation of logical and calculation errors in long arguments by external control via examples, experiments, and numerical checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warn that without checking by examples, 'after some ten pages half of all the signs in formulae will be wrong'; teach students to verify computations and to test the conclusions of proofs by concrete instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach problem-solving heuristics and techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate problem-solving methods and heuristic thinking (à la Polya) rather than rote theorem-proof rehearsal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend classical problem-solving literature (Polya's How to Solve It, Mathematics and Plausible Reasoning) and instruct students in searching for counterexamples, limits of applicability, and methodical exploration of special cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include significant theorems that convey mathematical natural science
rubrics_metrics.description: Present theorems of wide conceptual power (not merely 'sporting' results) that reveal connections across mathematics and applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: classification of surfaces is recommended for inclusion (even without proof) in high-school or university courses because it conveys the nature of mathematical discovery more effectively than isolated difficult proofs touted for publicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train computational and visualization skills (practical craft)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure students can perform concrete calculations and visual tasks (e.g., drawing parametric curves, visualizing Riemann surfaces) as essential parts of mathematical craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restore emphasis on skills historically considered necessary (times tables, drawing curves) and give exercises that require visualizing algebraic/geometric objects (xy = z^2, x = t^3 - 3t, y = t^4 - 2t^2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep mathematics tied to applications and avoid isolating it as mere recreation
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid presenting mathematics primarily as isolated achievements or 'rock-climbing' exercises disconnected from utility or broader scientific context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overemphasize publicity-friendly proofs of difficult theorems (e.g., Fermat) at the expense of showing why mathematics matters to other sciences and practical problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach classical, well-crafted texts and the historical canon
rubrics_metrics.description: Use and make students aware of influential, methodical works (Courant & Robbins, Rademacher & Töplitz, Hilbert & Cohn-Vossen, Polya, Klein, Hermite, Landau & Lifshitz) which present mathematics as connected, intuitive science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring back 'obsolete' but pedagogically rich texts rather than discarding them; encourage translations and dissemination of such works in local languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer concrete/local definitions over abstract axiomatics where pedagogically appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, give students concrete, workable definitions (e.g., manifolds as local graphs) before introducing abstract axiomatic generalisations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Whitney's theorem to justify presenting abstract manifolds as equivalence classes of concrete submanifolds; avoid burdening beginners with abstract axiomatic formulations that add little intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach the role and meaning of examples and counterexamples in forming conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sequences of examples and search for counterexamples to delimit the scope of empirical observations and to motivate precise conjectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrate with the example about partitions of consecutive odd numbers where a simple pattern breaks (1,2,4,8,16, then 29) to show the need for counterexamples in hypothesis formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose students to cross-field connections and interdisciplinarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage familiarity with neighbouring sciences (physics, biology) to prevent isolationism, to inform modeling choices, and to make mathematics more useful and intelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A teacher unfamiliar with basic physics (e.g., Landau & Lifshitz) will be unable to present many mathematical concepts meaningfully; stress cross-disciplinary literacy to maintain relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer operational/transformational viewpoints where illuminating
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce algebraic structures via their operations and natural occurrences (e.g., groups as transformations) rather than abstract axioms first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that 'axioms' are just obvious properties of transformations; cite Cayley's theorem that abstract groups are realizations of transformation groups to demystify abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize intuitive geometric/topological concepts early
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce students to topological/geometric constructs (Riemann surfaces, elliptic integrals, classification of surfaces) early to build a correct impression of modern mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out links like elliptic integrals giving motion times in Hamiltonian systems to show how geometry and topology connect to dynamics and applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warn against the 'absolutisation' of axioms and fetishising theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not teach axioms or theorems as absolute truths without discussing their domain of applicability and the danger of extrapolating beyond model validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite F. Klein's phrase 'The subtle poison of mathematical education' and discuss practical examples (mooring ships, landing craft) where naive application of idealised theorems fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage concise, example-driven presentations instead of long sterile proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor explanations that make concepts transparent through examples and intuition rather than long, formal deduction chains that obscure meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how e.g. the theory of determinants becomes clear when tied to oriented volume; avoid definitions that make basic properties (like commutativity of multiplication) seem puzzling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach error awareness and practical safeguards in lengthy formal arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Make students aware that long proofs and long computational chains are prone to logical and typographical errors, and teach methods to detect and guard against them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend routine cross-checks, examples, and experimental/numerical verification; emphasize that the longer and fancier the proof, the more vigilance required.
